result.relation_rationale: The article reports the requested PFS composite from random assignment to first PSA progression, radiographic progression, symptomatic deterioration, or death, comparing ADT plus orteronel with ADT plus bicalutamide. It reports the final analysis after 787 PFS events with median follow-up of 4.9 years. The analysis included 1,279 of 1,313 randomized participants, excluding 32 deemed ineligible and two who withdrew all consent before treatment, so its analyzed population is narrower than all randomized participants.

measurement.method: Time from random assignment to first documentation of PSA progression, radiologic progression, clinical progression (symptomatic deterioration), or death, whichever occurred first.

time_point_or_window.description: Time-to-event from random assignment through the final analysis; median follow-up 4.9 years.

target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups

reported.analysis_population: 1,279 participants included in the intention-to-treat analysis: 638 assigned to orteronel and 641 assigned to control; 32 randomized patients were ineligible and two withdrew all consent before starting treatment. PFS analysis followed 787 events (343 orteronel, 444 control); median follow-up was 4.9 years.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

Six hundred thirty-eight patients were randomly assigned to
the orteronel arm, and 641 were randomly assigned to the
control arm. At the cutoff date (February 5, 2021) for the
final analysis after 525 deaths (and 787 PFS events), the
median follow-up time was 4.9 years. Demographic and
clinical characteristics at baseline were well balanced
(Table 1). The median age of the patients for the orteronel
and control arms was 67.6 and 68.1 years, respectively.
Across both groups, approximately 10% of the patients
were African American, 49% had extensive disease, and
96% had a Zubrod performance status of 0 or 1.
Primary End Point
Analysis for OS occurred after the prespecified 525 deaths
were observed (251 in the orteronel group and 274 in the
control group). The median OS in the orteronel group was
81.1 months as compared with 70.2 months in the control
group. The OS rate at 5 years was 59.7% in the orteronel
group and 57.9% in the control group (HR for death 0.86;
95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). No statistically
significant improvement in OS was observed with orteronel
compared with control (Fig 1). This lack of treatment effect
on OS seemed consistent across stratification factors, in-
cluding disease severity, and by race (Fig 3 and Appendix
Table A3, online only).

Analysis of PFS occurred after 787 events were observed

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. sections.excerpt: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

2|Orteronel for Metastatic
3|Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer: A
4|Multicenter, Randomized, Open-Label Phase III
5|Trial (SWOG-1216)
6|Neeraj Agarwal, MD1; Catherine M. Tangen, DrPH2; Maha H.A. Hussain, MD3; Shilpa Gupta, MD4; Melissa Plets, MS2; Primo N. Lara, MD5;
7|Andrea L. Harzstark, MD6; Przemyslaw W. Twardowski, MD7; Channing J. Paller, MD8; Dylan Zylla, MD9; Matthew R. Zibelman, MD10;
8|Ellis Levine, MD11; Bruce J. Roth, MD12; Amir Goldkorn, MD13; Daniel A. Vaena, MD14,15; Manish Kohli, MD1,16; Tony Crispino17;
9|Nicholas J. Vogelzang, MD18; Ian M. Thompson Jr, MD19; and David I. Quinn, MD13
10|abstract
11|PURPOSE Orteronel (TAK-700) is a nonsteroidal 17,20-lyase inhibitor suppressing androgen synthesis. We
12|evaluated the clinical benefit of orteronel when added to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) in patients with
13|newly diagnosed metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.
14|METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
15|cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
16|with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
17|survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
18|P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
19|prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
20|RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
21|arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
22|follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
23|0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
24|81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
25|events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
26|was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.
27|CONCLUSION The study did not meet the primary end point of improved OS with orteronel. The lack of correlation
28|of PFS and PSA response with OS raises concerns over assumption of their consistent surrogacy for OS in the
29|context of extensive postprotocol therapy in this setting.
30|J Clin Oncol 40:3301-3309. © 2022 by American Society of Clinical Oncology
31|INTRODUCTION
32|The cornerstone of treatment for metastatic hormone-
33|sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) is androgen depri-
34|vation therapy (ADT) with medical or surgical castra-
35|tion.1 However, disease progression universally occurs
36|on ADT, mediated by extragonadal production of an-
37|drogens or androgen-independent activation of an-
38|drogen receptor.1 The treatment paradigm of mHSPC
39|has evolved over the past decade with multiple trials
40|showing improved survival by intensification of ADT with
41|either docetaxel chemotherapy or abiraterone, which
42|inhibits a pivotal enzyme in intra- and extragonadal
43|androgen synthesis (ie, CYP17 [CYP17 hydroxylase,
44|CYP17, 20 lyase]) located in the testes and adrenal
45|glands.1-5 More recently, two direct, potent, and specific
46|inhibitors of the androgen receptor, apalutamide and
47|enzalutamide, were approved on the basis of improved
48|survival in phase III trials.1,6,7 Currently, the most
49|common sequencing of these agents in the treatment of
50|metastatic prostate cancer is abiraterone acetate fol-
51|lowed by enzalutamide or docetaxel.8 One challenge
52|with abiraterone acetate is the requirement for coad-
53|ministration of corticosteroids because of inhibition of
54|CYP17 hydroxylase.1 This results in diminished cortisol
55|production and leads to secondary mineralocorticoid
56|excess, with symptoms such as electrolyte abnormali-
57|ties, hypertension, and edema.1
58|Orteronel (TAK-700) is a novel CYP17 inhibitor. In
59|comparison with abiraterone acetate, orteronel inhibits
60|CYP17, 20 lyase with greater specificity compared with
61|CYP17 hydroxylase and does not generally lead to the
62|syndrome of secondary mineralocorticoid excess.9,10

1|We hypothesized that the addition of orteronel to ADT would
2|improve overall survival (OS), progression-free survival
3|(PFS), and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response rela-
4|tive to bicalutamide with ADT among men with mHSPC.
5|METHODS
6|Trial Design and Conduct
7|The S1216 trial was a phase III, randomized, open-label,
8|multicenter trial involving patients with mHSPC. The trial
9|was designed by the SWOG study team and was approved
10|by the National Cancer Institute (NCI). Patients were en-
11|rolled
12|from
13|248
14|academic
15|and
16|community
17|centers
18|throughout the United States, incorporating three other
19|NCI-funded cooperative groups (ECOG-ACRIN, ALLIANCE,
20|and NRG). The NCI Central Institutional Review Board
21|approved the initial version of the Protocol (online only) and
22|all subsequent amendments. The study was conducted in
23|accordance with the International Conference on Harmo-
24|nization of Good Clinical Practice guidelines and the
25|principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Signed written
26|consent was obtained from all patients. First and last au-
27|thors (N.A. and D.I.Q.) and the statisticians (C.M.T. and
28|M.P.) among the authors assume responsibility for the
29|completeness and accuracy of the data and analyses and
30|for the fidelity of the trial to the Protocol.
31|Patients and Interventions
32|Eligible patients were required to have histologically con-
33|firmed adenocarcinoma of the prostate and metastatic
34|disease as evidenced by soft tissue and/or bony metasta-
35|ses. Enrolled patients had a Zubrod performance status of
36|0-2; a Zubrod performance status of 3 was allowed if from
37|bone pain only and a PSA $ 2.0 ng/mL. No other prior
38|systemic therapy for metastatic prostate cancer was
39|allowed (with the exception of up to 30 days of ADT for
40|metastatic disease before registration), and at least 6 months
41|must have elapsed since completion of prior neoadjuvant
42|and/or adjuvant ADT. Concomitant radiotherapy was allowed
43|only for baseline symptoms per investigator's clinical judg-
44|ment during the first 4 months of protocol treatment. Patients
45|who had not started any therapy with luteinizing hormone-
46|releasing hormone (LHRH) agonist, antagonist, or orchi-
47|ectomy (early induction group) and patients who had already
48|started therapy with LHRH agonist, antagonist, or orchi-
49|ectomy within 30 days before registration (late induction
50|group) were eligible. Patients who were deemed to have
51|extensive mHSPC were eligible for enrollment if, on the basis
52|of the judgment of the treating physician, they were un-
53|suitable candidates for docetaxel or if they declined doce-
54|taxel therapy.11
55|Exclusion criteria included brain metastases; prior therapy
56|with ketoconazole, abiraterone acetate, or enzalutamide;
57|New York Heart Association class III or IV heart failure at
58|screening or thromboembolic event; unstable angina
59|pectoris; myocardial infarction; or serious uncontrolled
60|cardiac arrhythmia # 6 months before registration.
61|Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive
62|orteronel (300 mg) orally twice daily or bicalutamide (50
63|mg) administered orally once daily, in addition to contin-
64|uous ADT. Patient assignment was dynamically balanced
65|on three stratification factors: severity of disease (minimal v
66|extensive), Zubrod performance status (0-1 v 2-3), and
67|preregistration treatment status (early v late induction).
68|Severity (or risk) of disease criteria in this study was orig-
69|inally reported in 1989, and since then, it has been used in
70|all SWOG trials in the mHSPC setting to date.11-13 Minimal
71|disease was defined as involvement of vertebrae and/or
72|pelvic bones and/or lymph nodes, and extensive disease
73|was defined as that with greater than minimal involvement.
74|Dynamic balancing is a general procedure for treatment
75|CONTEXT
76|Key Objective
77|We examined if adding orteronel, a novel androgen axis inhibitor, to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) would improve
78|outcomes compared with ADT plus bicalutamide in men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer in a phase III
79|trial.
80|Knowledge Generated
81|Addition of orteronel to ADT resulted in a significant improvement in progression-free survival and prostate-specific antigen
82|response but not in overall survival (OS), the primary end point. Interestingly, the median OS of patients in the control arm
83|of SWOG-1216 was 24 months higher than that in patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer on the
84|SWOG-9346 trial (reported in 2013) who had similar disease severity and also received ADT plus bicalutamide (70.2 v 46
85|months).
86|Relevance
87|These results indicate that orteronel is likely not an effective androgen axis inhibitor compared with recently approved agents
88|in this setting. Higher than anticipated OS of patients in the control arm is reflective of therapeutic advancements made
89|over the past decade in men with metastatic prostate cancer.

4|End Points
5|The primary end point was OS, which was defined as the time
6|from random assignment to the date of death from any cause.
7|Secondary end points were PFS, PSA response rates, and
8|adverse events (AEs) rate. PFS was defined as the time from
9|random assignment to first documentation of PSA progression
10|($ 25% increase and an absolute increase of at least 2 ng/mL
11|from the nadir PSA), radiologic progression (two or more new
12|lesions on radionuclide bone scans, per Prostate Cancer
13|Working Group 2 [PCWG2] criteria, and/or soft tissue pro-
14|gression per RECIST version 1.1), clinical progression
15|(symptomatic deterioration) or death, whichever occurred
16|first. PSA response rates were divided into complete response
17|(CR; PSA , 0.2 ng/mL), partial response (PR; PSA between
18|0.2 and 4.0 ng/mL), and no response (NR; PSA . 4.0 ng/mL)
19|at a 7-month landmark after random assignment.
20|Assessments
21|Patients were assessed for efficacy according to the
22|modified RECIST version 1.1 with the use of computed
23|tomography or magnetic resonance imaging of the chest,
24|abdomen, and pelvis during screening (# 6 weeks be-
25|fore random assignment) and according to PCWG2
26|criteria with the use of bone scanning.15 Progression
27|events were assessed by the treating investigator.

30|plus bicalutamide was assumed to be 54 months on the

33|the intermittent v continuous ADT phase III trial, and an
34|additional 6 months from the newer drug approvals in the
35|castrate-resistant setting, which may extend survival).11

4|Subsequent Life-Prolonging Anticancer Therapy
5|Treatment after discontinuation of protocol therapy was
6|initiated per patient's choice and as per local standard of
7|care. At the time of this report, receipt of at least one ap-
8|proved life-prolonging therapy after discontinuation of pro-
9|tocol therapy was evaluable in 331 patients in the orteronel
10|arm and 402 patients in the control arm. A higher proportion
11|of patients in the control arm received postprotocol therapy,
12|which was consistent with a higher incidence of disease
13|progression in the control arm. Of these, 203 (61.3%) pa-
14|tients in the orteronel arm and 311 (77.4%) patients in the
15|control arm received one or more life-prolonging anticancer
16|therapies (Appendix Table A1, online only).
17|DISCUSSION
18|In this study, addition of orteronel to ADT compared with
19|bicalutamide led to a statistically significant improvement in
20|PFS and PSA response. Although the approximately 11-
21|month improvement in median OS with orteronel appears
22|clinically meaningful, it did not reach the prespecified re-
23|quirement for statistical significance. The assumption of 54-
24|month OS for the control arm was a substantial underesti-
25|mate, exceeded by 16 months in the actual results, chal-
26|lenging the probability of a statistically significant result.
27|The discrepancy between improvement in PFS but not in
28|OS might have occurred because of receipt of subsequent
29|life-prolonging therapy in a large proportion of patients in
30|the control arm. The primary end point of OS evaluated not
31|only the benefit of early addition of orteronel but also the
32|impact of subsequent life-prolonging therapies including
33|abiraterone acetate, enzalutamide, docetaxel, cabazitaxel,
34|sipuleucel-T, and radium-223.16-23 In this study, 77.4% of
35|the patients who progressed in the control arm received
36|subsequent life-prolonging therapies compared with 21%-
37|64% of patients in phase III studies in this setting reported
38|since 2013 where the control arm comprised ADT only
39|without recently approved novel agents (nonintensified
40|ADT; Appendix Table A2, online only). The receipt of
41|subsequent life-prolonging therapies by the majority of
42|patients on the control arm might have also resulted in an
43|absolute median OS of 70 months, the highest ever reported
44|for patients on a nonintensified ADT control arm of con-
45|temporary trials in mHSPC. It is also possible that the results
46|from the CHAARTED trial, which reported approximately
47|1 year after activation of SWOG-1216 and showed signifi-
48|cant improvement in OS with docetaxel in patients with
49|high-volume disease, prompted a preferential recruitment
50|of patients with low-volume disease on the SWOG-1216
51|trial, leading to an unexpected improvement in the OS in
52|both arms, especially in the control arm. For example, the
53|median OS in patients with low-volume mHSPC in the
54|CHAARTED trial had not been reached after a median
55|follow-up of 53.7 months and was 83.4 months in the
56|GETUG AFU-15 trial.24,25 Nonetheless, when compared
57|with the median OS of men on the SWOG-9346 trial in the
58|mHSPC setting (reported in 2013), where all patients re-
59|ceived ADT plus bicalutamide and which had almost an
60|identical proportion of men with extensive disease by SWOG
61|criteria of disease severity (48% v 49%), the median OS in
62|the control arm of SWOG-1216 was 24 months higher (46 v
63|70.2 months) (Appendix Figure A2).11

1|SWOG-1216 is the third phaseIII trial investigating the use of
2|orteronel in the metastatic prostate cancer setting after the
3|ELM-PC5 and ELM-PC4 trials failed to meet their primary
4|end point of OS. The ELM-PC5 trial was conducted in the
5|postdocetaxel
6|metastatic
7|castration-resistant
8|prostate
9|cancer (mCRPC) setting, whereas ELM-PC4 trial was
10|conducted in the predocetaxel mCRPC setting.26,27 Re-
11|sults of these three trials, which combined and enrolled
12|more than 3000 patients with metastatic prostate cancer,
13|suggest that orteronel is likely not an effective androgen
14|axis inhibitor compared with recently approved agents
15|such as abiraterone, apalutamide, and enzalutamide.
16|Furthermore, both PFS and OS were significantly im-
17|proved with addition of abiraterone, apalutamide, and
18|enzalutamide to ADT compared with ADT alone in the
19|LATITUDE, TITAN, and the ARCHES trials, respectively,
20|all conducted in the mHSPC setting (Appendix Table A2).
21|The strengths of this study include enrollment of patients from
22|academic and community centers across the United States,
23|proportionate representation of African-American patients
24|(highest to date among all contemporary trials), and a rep-
25|resentative patient population as evident by the risk status
26|(approximately 50% high risk). These results emphasize the
27|need to account for receipt of subsequent life-prolonging
28|therapy and a need for validated surrogate intermediate
29|end points to expedite drug development in a time where the
30|treatment paradigm in the mCRPC setting is rapidly changing.
31|Given the improved OS in men with mHSPC receiving non-
32|intensified therapy, it may also be prudent to focus on de-
33|signing trials for those at the highest risk of early disease
34|progression and death. The results of SWOG-1216 indicate
35|that access to life-prolonging therapies, approved over the
36|past decade, has significantly improved outcomes in patients
37|with metastatic prostate cancer. Furthermore, this trial pro-
38|vides survival estimates in the contemporary era when pa-
39|tients with mHSPC have access to multiple approved life-
40|prolonging therapies. These contemporary survival data will
41|be invaluable for counseling of patients with newly diagnosed
42|mHSPC and for design of future clinical trials in this setting.

answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.

This is a question about baseline imbalance suggesting a randomization problem, not about how the sequence was generated or whether allocation was concealed. Do not use the baseline table to backfill either process question.
This answer must not alter answers about sequence generation or concealment.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
invalid_shortcuts: statistical significance of one isolated comparison
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.

on three stratification factors: severity of disease (minimal v
extensive), Zubrod performance status (0-1 v 2-3), and
preregistration treatment status (early v late induction).

inally reported in 1989, and since then, it has been used in
all SWOG trials in the mHSPC setting to date.11-13 Minimal
disease was defined as involvement of vertebrae and/or
pelvic bones and/or lymph nodes, and extensive disease
was defined as that with greater than minimal involvement.

original reports
Orteronel for Metastatic
Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer: A
Multicenter, Randomized, Open-Label Phase III
Trial (SWOG-1216)
Neeraj Agarwal, MD1; Catherine M. Tangen, DrPH2; Maha H.A. Hussain, MD3; Shilpa Gupta, MD4; Melissa Plets, MS2; Primo N. Lara, MD5;
Andrea L. Harzstark, MD6; Przemyslaw W. Twardowski, MD7; Channing J. Paller, MD8; Dylan Zylla, MD9; Matthew R. Zibelman, MD10;
Ellis Levine, MD11; Bruce J. Roth, MD12; Amir Goldkorn, MD13; Daniel A. Vaena, MD14,15; Manish Kohli, MD1,16; Tony Crispino17;
Nicholas J. Vogelzang, MD18; Ian M. Thompson Jr, MD19; and David I. Quinn, MD13
abstract
PURPOSE Orteronel (TAK-700) is a nonsteroidal 17,20-lyase inhibitor suppressing androgen synthesis. We
evaluated the clinical benefit of orteronel when added to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) in patients with
newly diagnosed metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.
METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.
CONCLUSION The study did not meet the primary end point of improved OS with orteronel. The lack of correlation
of PFS and PSA response with OS raises concerns over assumption of their consistent surrogacy for OS in the
context of extensive postprotocol therapy in this setting.

INTRODUCTION
The cornerstone of treatment for metastatic hormone-
sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) is androgen depri-
vation therapy (ADT) with medical or surgical castra-
tion.1 However, disease progression universally occurs
on ADT, mediated by extragonadal production of an-
drogens or androgen-independent activation of an-
drogen receptor.1 The treatment paradigm of mHSPC
has evolved over the past decade with multiple trials
showing improved survival by intensification of ADT with
either docetaxel chemotherapy or abiraterone, which
inhibits a pivotal enzyme in intra- and extragonadal
androgen synthesis (ie, CYP17 [CYP17 hydroxylase,
CYP17, 20 lyase]) located in the testes and adrenal
glands.1-5 More recently, two direct, potent, and specific
inhibitors of the androgen receptor, apalutamide and
enzalutamide, were approved on the basis of improved
survival in phase III trials.1,6,7 Currently, the most
common sequencing of these agents in the treatment of
metastatic prostate cancer is abiraterone acetate fol-
lowed by enzalutamide or docetaxel.8 One challenge
with abiraterone acetate is the requirement for coad-
ministration of corticosteroids because of inhibition of
CYP17 hydroxylase.1 This results in diminished cortisol
production and leads to secondary mineralocorticoid
excess, with symptoms such as electrolyte abnormali-
ties, hypertension, and edema.1
Orteronel (TAK-700) is a novel CYP17 inhibitor. In
comparison with abiraterone acetate, orteronel inhibits
CYP17, 20 lyase with greater specificity compared with
CYP17 hydroxylase and does not generally lead to the
syndrome of secondary mineralocorticoid excess.9,10

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.

A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

Orteronel for Metastatic
Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer: A
Multicenter, Randomized, Open-Label Phase III
Trial (SWOG-1216)
Neeraj Agarwal, MD1; Catherine M. Tangen, DrPH2; Maha H.A. Hussain, MD3; Shilpa Gupta, MD4; Melissa Plets, MS2; Primo N. Lara, MD5;
Andrea L. Harzstark, MD6; Przemyslaw W. Twardowski, MD7; Channing J. Paller, MD8; Dylan Zylla, MD9; Matthew R. Zibelman, MD10;
Ellis Levine, MD11; Bruce J. Roth, MD12; Amir Goldkorn, MD13; Daniel A. Vaena, MD14,15; Manish Kohli, MD1,16; Tony Crispino17;
Nicholas J. Vogelzang, MD18; Ian M. Thompson Jr, MD19; and David I. Quinn, MD13
abstract
PURPOSE Orteronel (TAK-700) is a nonsteroidal 17,20-lyase inhibitor suppressing androgen synthesis. We
evaluated the clinical benefit of orteronel when added to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) in patients with
newly diagnosed metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.
METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.
CONCLUSION The study did not meet the primary end point of improved OS with orteronel. The lack of correlation
of PFS and PSA response with OS raises concerns over assumption of their consistent surrogacy for OS in the
context of extensive postprotocol therapy in this setting.

The cornerstone of treatment for metastatic hormone-
sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) is androgen depri-
vation therapy (ADT) with medical or surgical castra-
tion.1 However, disease progression universally occurs
on ADT, mediated by extragonadal production of an-
drogens or androgen-independent activation of an-
drogen receptor.1 The treatment paradigm of mHSPC
has evolved over the past decade with multiple trials
showing improved survival by intensification of ADT with
either docetaxel chemotherapy or abiraterone, which
inhibits a pivotal enzyme in intra- and extragonadal
androgen synthesis (ie, CYP17 [CYP17 hydroxylase,
CYP17, 20 lyase]) located in the testes and adrenal
glands.1-5 More recently, two direct, potent, and specific
inhibitors of the androgen receptor, apalutamide and
enzalutamide, were approved on the basis of improved
survival in phase III trials.1,6,7 Currently, the most
common sequencing of these agents in the treatment of
metastatic prostate cancer is abiraterone acetate fol-
lowed by enzalutamide or docetaxel.8 One challenge
with abiraterone acetate is the requirement for coad-
ministration of corticosteroids because of inhibition of
CYP17 hydroxylase.1 This results in diminished cortisol
production and leads to secondary mineralocorticoid
excess, with symptoms such as electrolyte abnormali-
ties, hypertension, and edema.1
Orteronel (TAK-700) is a novel CYP17 inhibitor. In
comparison with abiraterone acetate, orteronel inhibits
CYP17, 20 lyase with greater specificity compared with
CYP17 hydroxylase and does not generally lead to the
syndrome of secondary mineralocorticoid excess.9,10

answers.justification: The main article explicitly describes S1216 as an open-label randomized trial. Participants received visibly different regimens—orteronel twice daily versus bicalutamide once daily with ADT—so participants were aware of their assignments.
The trial was open-label, and clinicians assessed progression events. With the different assigned medicines and dosing schedules visible, the treating personnel were aware of assignments.

bases.unresolved_premise: Whether open-label conduct led participants or staff to make protocol-inconsistent treatment changes because of the trial context.
bases.stopping_rationale: I inspected the protocol's treatment, dose-modification, drug-compliance, and removal rules, plus the article's CONSORT reasons for treatment discontinuation. The reported reasons largely include progression, toxicity, death, and patient refusal; the protocol permits removal for progression or symptomatic deterioration, toxicity, new systemic treatment, and withdrawal. The report does not identify any protocol-inconsistent changes or link changes to trial context. The remaining 'other' discontinuation categories and unreported conduct prevent a probable judgment in either direction.

answers.justification: Open-label awareness is clear, but it does not establish trial-context-caused departures. Protocol rules permit treatment changes or removal for progression, toxicity, new systemic treatment, and patient withdrawal, and observed discontinuations include progression, adverse events, death, and refusal. The report does not clarify the 'other' categories or identify prohibited deviations caused by the trial context, so neither probable direction is supported.
unknowns: Whether any protocol-inconsistent treatment change occurred because of the open-label trial context; what the unclassified 'other' discontinuations comprised.

answers.justification: The report analyzed participants by randomized group and describes the analysis as intention-to-treat. The 32 exclusions were identified as ineligible at baseline, and two participants withdrew all consent before starting treatment. unknowns: The report does not provide a fuller analysis-population rationale for the 32 ineligible participants, but it identifies them as ineligible and gives the exclusion reasons.

The analysis included 1,279 of 1,313 randomized participants, excluding 32 deemed ineligible and two who withdrew all consent before treatment, so its analyzed population is narrower than all randomized participants.

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
The report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Neutral paired control: complete ascertainment and an analysis denominator with unresolved ascertainment differ only in the availability premise; administrative censoring and worsening-related follow-up loss differ only in the missingness mechanism.

Six hundred thirty-eight patients were randomly assigned to

control arm. At the cutoff date (February 5, 2021) for the

clinical characteristics at baseline were well balanced
(Table 1). The median age of the patients for the orteronel
and control arms was 67.6 and 68.1 years, respectively.
Across both groups, approximately 10% of the patients
were African American, 49% had extensive disease, and
96% had a Zubrod performance status of 0 or 1.

were observed (251 in the orteronel group and 274 in the
control group). The median OS in the orteronel group was
81.1 months as compared with 70.2 months in the control
group. The OS rate at 5 years was 59.7% in the orteronel
group and 57.9% in the control group (HR for death 0.86;
95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). No statistically
significant improvement in OS was observed with orteronel
compared with control (Fig 1). This lack of treatment effect
on OS seemed consistent across stratification factors, in-
cluding disease severity, and by race (Fig 3 and Appendix
Table A3, online only).

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

Orteronel for Metastatic
Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer: A
Multicenter, Randomized, Open-Label Phase III
Trial (SWOG-1216)
Neeraj Agarwal, MD1; Catherine M. Tangen, DrPH2; Maha H.A. Hussain, MD3; Shilpa Gupta, MD4; Melissa Plets, MS2; Primo N. Lara, MD5;
Andrea L. Harzstark, MD6; Przemyslaw W. Twardowski, MD7; Channing J. Paller, MD8; Dylan Zylla, MD9; Matthew R. Zibelman, MD10;
Ellis Levine, MD11; Bruce J. Roth, MD12; Amir Goldkorn, MD13; Daniel A. Vaena, MD14,15; Manish Kohli, MD1,16; Tony Crispino17;
Nicholas J. Vogelzang, MD18; Ian M. Thompson Jr, MD19; and David I. Quinn, MD13
abstract
PURPOSE Orteronel (TAK-700) is a nonsteroidal 17,20-lyase inhibitor suppressing androgen synthesis. We
evaluated the clinical benefit of orteronel when added to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) in patients with
newly diagnosed metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.
METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.
CONCLUSION The study did not meet the primary end point of improved OS with orteronel. The lack of correlation
of PFS and PSA response with OS raises concerns over assumption of their consistent surrogacy for OS in the
context of extensive postprotocol therapy in this setting.
J Clin Oncol 40:3301-3309. © 2022 by American Society of Clinical Oncology
INTRODUCTION
The cornerstone of treatment for metastatic hormone-
sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) is androgen depri-
vation therapy (ADT) with medical or surgical castra-
tion.1 However, disease progression universally occurs
on ADT, mediated by extragonadal production of an-
drogens or androgen-independent activation of an-
drogen receptor.1 The treatment paradigm of mHSPC
has evolved over the past decade with multiple trials
showing improved survival by intensification of ADT with
either docetaxel chemotherapy or abiraterone, which
inhibits a pivotal enzyme in intra- and extragonadal
androgen synthesis (ie, CYP17 [CYP17 hydroxylase,
CYP17, 20 lyase]) located in the testes and adrenal
glands.1-5 More recently, two direct, potent, and specific
inhibitors of the androgen receptor, apalutamide and
enzalutamide, were approved on the basis of improved
survival in phase III trials.1,6,7 Currently, the most
common sequencing of these agents in the treatment of
metastatic prostate cancer is abiraterone acetate fol-
lowed by enzalutamide or docetaxel.8 One challenge
with abiraterone acetate is the requirement for coad-
ministration of corticosteroids because of inhibition of
CYP17 hydroxylase.1 This results in diminished cortisol
production and leads to secondary mineralocorticoid
excess, with symptoms such as electrolyte abnormali-
ties, hypertension, and edema.1
Orteronel (TAK-700) is a novel CYP17 inhibitor. In
comparison with abiraterone acetate, orteronel inhibits
CYP17, 20 lyase with greater specificity compared with
CYP17 hydroxylase and does not generally lead to the
syndrome of secondary mineralocorticoid excess.9,10

result.relation_rationale: The article reports the requested PFS composite from random assignment to first PSA progression, radiographic progression, symptomatic deterioration, or death, comparing ADT plus orteronel with ADT plus bicalutamide. It reports the final analysis after 787 PFS events with median follow-up of 4.9 years. The analysis included 1,279 of 1,313 randomized participants, excluding 32 deemed ineligible and two who withdrew all consent before treatment, so its analyzed population is narrower than all randomized participants.

measurement.method: Time from random assignment to first documentation of PSA progression, radiologic progression, clinical progression (symptomatic deterioration), or death, whichever occurred first.

time_point_or_window.description: Time-to-event from random assignment through the final analysis; median follow-up 4.9 years.

target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups

reported.analysis_population: 1,279 participants included in the intention-to-treat analysis: 638 assigned to orteronel and 641 assigned to control; 32 randomized patients were ineligible and two withdrew all consent before starting treatment. PFS analysis followed 787 events (343 orteronel, 444 control); median follow-up was 4.9 years.

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
The report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Neutral paired control: complete ascertainment and an analysis denominator with unresolved ascertainment differ only in the availability premise; administrative censoring and worsening-related follow-up loss differ only in the missingness mechanism.
invalid_shortcuts: analysis denominators or ITT membership alone
an event count treated as an observed-outcome count
an analysis denominator treated as an outcome denominator
a generic censoring rule without actual rates or follow-up accounting
imputed data counted as observed outcomes

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.2
sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
sections.excerpt: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.

sections.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 45-46, Box 8, signalling question 3.4
sections.excerpt: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.

answer_anchors.text: A bias-correcting or informative sensitivity analysis indicates the result was not biased.
The available evidence does not show that the result was free from missing-data bias.

questions.bias_construct: Whether there is evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data.
considerations: Imputation alone is not evidence that missing outcome data did not bias the result.

Availability and mitigation are separate premises: a familiar method name or numerically stable estimate is not enough; the sensitivity analysis must span plausible assumptions relevant to the documented missingness mechanism.
This question permits complete ascertainment, mechanism-matched reassurance, and legitimate uncertainty. Do not apply a universal percentage threshold in place of a Result-specific impact judgment.
questions.decision_rule: Evidence may come from methods correcting for bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions about missingness and true outcome. The assumptions must match the documented missingness mechanism and the approved Result. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source explicitly establishes that relationship. Last-observation-carried-forward or multiple imputation based only on intervention group should not be assumed to correct bias.
evidence_needed: A bias-correcting analysis or sensitivity analysis with plausible missingness assumptions and its result, including the missingness mechanism it addresses.
If the source only changes intervention-group attribution or analysis membership, record that distinction; do not describe it as a test of unobserved outcome values without source support.
invalid_shortcuts: multiple imputation based only on intervention group
questions.no_information_rule: No_information is not an allowed response to this question in the parallel-assignment pack; provide direct evidence or answer no/probably no.

However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

questions.wording: If N/PN/NI to 3.1: Is there evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data?

answer_anchors.text: Missingness could depend on the true outcome value.
Documented missingness reasons are unrelated to the outcome.

questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value.
considerations: For time-to-event outcomes, inspect censoring reasons and timing to identify missing follow-up. A common administrative cutoff does not by itself establish outcome-dependent missingness.

Separate observed outcome data, analysed membership, follow-up availability, and the missingness mechanism. Treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring is not by itself evidence that observation stopped. This question asks whether the missingness mechanism could depend on the true value; it is not a question about analysis membership.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when loss to follow-up or withdrawal could relate to health status or outcome. Answer no or probably no when all missingness had documented reasons unrelated to outcome, such as a failed measuring device or interruption to routine data collection.
evidence_needed: Reasons for missingness and their relationship to participants' health status or true outcome, including censoring and treatment switching in time-to-event analyses.
invalid_shortcuts: a reason for withdrawal without its relation to outcome
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the reasons for missingness do not permit assessment of dependence on the true value.
questions.official_guidance: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.3
questions.wording: If N/PN to 3.2: Could missingness in the outcome depend on its true value?

answer_anchors.text: Missingness likely depended on the true outcome value.
The analysis accounted for characteristics explaining the relationship, or dependence was not likely.

questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness that could depend on true value likely depended on it.
considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Judge likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances; absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Keep the stages distinct: observed outcome data and follow-up availability describe what was obtained; 3.3 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value; 3.4 asks whether that dependence was likely. Do not promote possible dependence to likely dependence without supporting evidence.
questions.decision_rule: Consider differences in missingness or censoring rates, reasons that depend on true value, reasons differing between groups, trial circumstances, and censoring after stopping or changing intervention. Answer no when analysis accounted for participant characteristics likely to explain the relationship.
evidence_needed: Group-specific missingness or censoring, reasons for missingness, trial circumstances, and any analysis accounting for relevant participant characteristics.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when likelihood of dependence on true value cannot be judged from the available evidence.
questions.official_guidance: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 45-46, Box 8, signalling question 3.4
questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 3.3: Is it likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value?

Multicenter, Randomized, Open-Label Phase III

Neeraj Agarwal, MD1; Catherine M. Tangen, DrPH2; Maha H.A. Hussain, MD3; Shilpa Gupta, MD4; Melissa Plets, MS2; Primo N. Lara, MD5;

abstract
PURPOSE Orteronel (TAK-700) is a nonsteroidal 17,20-lyase inhibitor suppressing androgen synthesis. We
evaluated the clinical benefit of orteronel when added to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) in patients with
newly diagnosed metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.
METHODS In this open-label randomized phase III study, patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate
cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to ADT with orteronel (300 mg oral twice daily; experimental arm) or ADT
with bicalutamide (50 mg oral once daily; control arm). The primary objective was the comparison of overall
survival (OS), targeting a 33% improvement in median survival. A stratified log-rank test with a one-sided
P # .022 would indicate statistical significance. Secondary end points were progression-free survival (PFS),
prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level at 7 months (# 0.2 v 0.2 to # 4 v . 4 ng/mL), and adverse event profile.
RESULTS Among 1,279 patients included in the analysis, 638 were randomly assigned to the ADT plus orteronel
arm and 641 to the control arm. The median age was 68 years; 49% had extensive disease. After a median
follow-up of 4.9 years, there was a significant improvement in PFS (median 47.6 v 23.0 months, hazard ratio
0.58; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.67; P , .0001) and PSA response at 7 months (P , .0001), but not in OS (median
81.1 v 70.2 months, hazard ratio 0.86; 95% CI, 0.72 to 1.02; P 5 .040, one-sided). More grade 3/4 adverse
events occurred in the experimental versus the control arms (43% v 14%). Postprotocol life-prolonging therapy
was received by 77.4% of patients in the control arm and 61.3% of patients in the orteronel arm.
CONCLUSION The study did not meet the primary end point of improved OS with orteronel. The lack of correlation
of PFS and PSA response with OS raises concerns over assumption of their consistent surrogacy for OS in the
context of extensive postprotocol therapy in this setting.
J Clin Oncol 40:3301-3309. © 2022 by American Society of Clinical Oncology
INTRODUCTION
The cornerstone of treatment for metastatic hormone-
sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC) is androgen depri-
vation therapy (ADT) with medical or surgical castra-
tion.1 However, disease progression universally occurs
on ADT, mediated by extragonadal production of an-
drogens or androgen-independent activation of an-
drogen receptor.1 The treatment paradigm of mHSPC
has evolved over the past decade with multiple trials
showing improved survival by intensification of ADT with
either docetaxel chemotherapy or abiraterone, which
inhibits a pivotal enzyme in intra- and extragonadal
androgen synthesis (ie, CYP17 [CYP17 hydroxylase,
CYP17, 20 lyase]) located in the testes and adrenal
glands.1-5 More recently, two direct, potent, and specific
inhibitors of the androgen receptor, apalutamide and
enzalutamide, were approved on the basis of improved
survival in phase III trials.1,6,7 Currently, the most
common sequencing of these agents in the treatment of
metastatic prostate cancer is abiraterone acetate fol-
lowed by enzalutamide or docetaxel.8 One challenge
with abiraterone acetate is the requirement for coad-
ministration of corticosteroids because of inhibition of
CYP17 hydroxylase.1 This results in diminished cortisol
production and leads to secondary mineralocorticoid
excess, with symptoms such as electrolyte abnormali-
ties, hypertension, and edema.1
Orteronel (TAK-700) is a novel CYP17 inhibitor. In
comparison with abiraterone acetate, orteronel inhibits
CYP17, 20 lyase with greater specificity compared with
CYP17 hydroxylase and does not generally lead to the
syndrome of secondary mineralocorticoid excess.9,10
